The filter media has been lost and the bed is too shallow
The settled water is carrying excessive solids to the filter

The media is dissolving in the treated water

A hydraulic surge has cracked deposits loose from the media
The filter is still ripening after its last backwash
Air binding is forcing water around the media

Archived backwash air release notes

The media is breaking down and releasing sand into the effluent
The settled water quality collapses after every backwash
The underdrains are failing progressively

Archived underdrain inspection report

tasks.prompt: A large water main has broken on a commercial street. Before the repair is finished, the utility must judge the contamination risk to the surrounding area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Pressure in the area around the break fell to zero, and some nearby services briefly showed negative pressure as the main drained.
The excavation pit contains muddy groundwater standing around the exposed, opened pipe ends.
Customers near the break report air and discoloured water as pressure returns.
The break section was a through main serving about 200 homes, now isolated by closed valves.
Chlorine residual in the surrounding mains was normal before the break.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Loss of pressure around an open main in muddy groundwater creates a real intrusion risk, so the repaired section and nearby services need disinfection, flushing, and sampling before normal use
There is no contamination risk because the water was chlorinated before the break
The only concern is low pressure; the water quality cannot be affected by a break
Contamination is certain throughout the whole town system

inference.explanation: Pressure fell to zero and went negative nearby, the opened pipe sits in muddy groundwater, and air and discolouration appear as pressure returns. Intrusion during the pressure loss is the supported risk, calling for disinfection, flushing, and sampling of the affected area. Prior chlorination does not protect an open, depressurized main, pressure loss plainly can affect quality, and a town-wide certainty overstates an isolated section.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the precaution approach for this break class?

options.label: Archived main break repair and sampling records for past depressurized breaks
Archived pre-break residual results
Archived town-wide bacteriological summary

nextClue.explanation: Past break records show the disinfection, flushing, and sampling steps used after depressurized repairs.

clueText.nc-a: Past records show every depressurized break section was disinfected, flushed, and sampled clear before return to normal service, with advisories used when sampling could not clear the area promptly.
clueText.nc-b: Pre-break residuals were normal, which did not remove the need for post-repair sampling in those cases.
clueText.nc-c: Town-wide summaries stayed normal in past events because the affected sections were isolated and handled locally.

tasks.prompt: An elevated tank delivers water that alternates between fresh and stale: morning draws taste flat with low residual, while afternoon water seems fresher.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Temperature probes show the tank water layered: a warm top layer over a cold bottom layer, with a sharp change between.
Residual samples from the top of the tank read much lower than samples from the bottom.
The tank fills and draws through a single common pipe at the bottom, with no mixing system installed.
Level records show the tank rarely drops below three quarters full, so the top layer can sit for many days.
The tank was designed before the current demand pattern, and daily demand now uses only a small part of its volume.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The tank is stratifying and short-circuiting through its bottom pipe, so the oldest top layer only leaves when levels swing widely
The tank coating is consuming chlorine from the water
The plant is sending alternating batches of good and bad water
The sample taps on the tank are faulty

inference.explanation: Layered temperatures, lower residual at the top, a single bottom fill-and-draw pipe, and a level that rarely drops mean the top layer ages in place. That is stratification with poor turnover. A coating effect would not layer by temperature, plant batches would show at the plant, and two sample depths agreeing with the layering clears the taps.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the stratification pattern?

options.label: Archived tank temperature and residual profiles by depth across seasons
Archived tank coating inspection report
Archived plant production quality log

nextClue.explanation: Depth profiles across seasons show the layering and residual gap repeating.

clueText.nc-a: Profiles show the same warm, low-residual top layer forming every summer and breaking down only after large level swings in autumn.
clueText.nc-b: The coating inspection found the lining intact and inert.
clueText.nc-c: Plant production quality is steady day to day, so the variation develops inside the tank.

tasks.prompt: An elevated tank is found overflowing at its vent on a quiet night, although its level instrument shows the tank only 60 percent full.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A manual tape measurement at the tank reads essentially full, matching the overflow, not the instrument.
The instrument float is found coated with ice and slime and moves stiffly in its guide.
High-level alarm records show the alarm never triggered during the fill.
Inlet pumps ran their normal cycle and shut off on a timer, not on the level signal, during control maintenance.
The level reading had been drifting slowly downward relative to manual checks for weeks.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The level instrument is reading falsely low because its float is fouled, so the tank filled past its real top
The inlet pumps have suddenly doubled their capacity
The tank has shrunk and holds less than its rated volume
The overflow pipe has been blocked and is spraying water

inference.explanation: Manual measurement says full, the float is iced and slimed and stiff, the high alarm never fired, pumps ran on timer, and the reading had drifted for weeks. That is a fouled level instrument. Pump capacity did not change, tanks do not shrink, and water at the vent is a genuine overflow, not a blocked pipe spray.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the instrument drift?

options.label: Archived level instrument versus manual gauge comparison checks
Archived pump capacity test results
Archived tank capacity drawings

nextClue.explanation: Comparison checks document the gap between instrument and manual readings growing over time.

clueText.nc-a: Checks show the instrument reading 5 percent low a month ago and 25 percent low last week against the tape, a steady fouling drift.
clueText.nc-b: Pump tests show normal capacity, and pumps stopped on schedule.
clueText.nc-c: Capacity drawings confirm the tank volume, and the tape reading fits it.

tasks.prompt: Through a warm summer, one storage-heavy part of the system using chloramine residual keeps losing total chlorine, and nitrite keeps appearing at the same sampling points.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Affected sites have the oldest water age in the system, downstream of a large storage tank.
Ammonia at those sites is falling while nitrite rises, a pattern that progresses through the summer.
Heterotrophic plate counts at the affected sites are elevated compared with the rest of the system.
Sites with young water near the plant hold their chloramine residual normally.
Water temperatures at the affected sites reach 26 C.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Nitrifying bacteria in the warm, old water are consuming ammonia and chloramine and producing nitrite
The plant is failing to add enough chloramine for the whole system
Sunlight is destroying the residual inside the buried mains
The nitrite results are a sampling preservative error

inference.explanation: The oldest, warmest sites lose ammonia as nitrite rises, plate counts are elevated there, and young-water sites hold residual normally. That is biological nitrification in the system. A plant dosing failure would show at young sites too, buried mains see no sunlight, and a preservative error would not track water age and temperature.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the nitrification pattern?

options.label: Archived ammonia, nitrite, and residual results by site across past summers
Archived plant chloramine dose log
Archived sampling preservative lot records

nextClue.explanation: Site results across summers show nitrification starting at the oldest sites each warm season.

clueText.nc-a: Past summers show the same sequence at the same sites: ammonia falling, nitrite rising, then residual loss, beginning weeks after water passed 20 C.
clueText.nc-b: Plant dose logs are steady, and young sites prove the dose is adequate.
clueText.nc-c: Preservative lots changed mid-season in past years without changing the pattern.

tasks.prompt: A car wash reports its rinse water smells of solvent, and two nearby businesses report a chemical taste, all on the same afternoon a nearby watermain pressure transient occurred.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A pressure logger shows a brief negative pressure dip in the area main during a pump trip at the plant.
The car wash has a chemical feed connected to its water line, and its backflow preventer test port shows it failed its last test and was never repaired.
Samples from the affected businesses show the same solvent-like character as the car wash chemical diluted in water.
Homes upstream of the car wash on the same main report no taste problems.
Plant treated water and the rest of the system test and taste normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: During the pressure dip, chemical was drawn back from the car wash through its failed backflow preventer into the local main
The treatment plant accidentally dosed solvent into the water
A fuel spill has entered the whole distribution system
The taste is caused by the plant normal chlorine dose

inference.explanation: A negative pressure dip occurred, the car wash chemical system has a failed and unrepaired backflow preventer, affected samples match that chemical, and upstream homes are clear. That is backflow at the car wash. The plant and the rest of the system are normal, ruling out plant dosing and a system-wide spill, and chlorine does not smell of solvent.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the backflow path?

options.label: Archived backflow preventer test and repair records for the premises on this main
Archived plant chemical inventory
Archived system-wide complaint log

nextClue.explanation: Preventer records for the street show which device was failed and overdue at the time.

clueText.nc-a: Records show the car wash preventer failed its test 14 months ago with no repair filed, while neighbouring premises devices passed on schedule.
clueText.nc-b: Plant inventory contains no solvent chemical of the type tasted.
clueText.nc-c: The complaint log shows the event confined to premises downstream of the car wash.

tasks.prompt: A hilltop neighbourhood wakes to no water at all, although the treatment plant produced normally all night.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The booster pump station feeding the hilltop zone shows both pumps tripped on an electrical fault at about 02:00.
The small zone tank level fell steadily from 02:00 and reached empty near 06:00, when taps ran dry.
The zone below the hill, fed directly, kept normal pressure all night.
The pump station alarm dialer was out of service, so the trip raised no callout.
No main breaks or valve closures are found in the zone.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The booster pumps tripped and, with no alarm callout, the zone tank drained until the hilltop ran dry
A major main break emptied the zone overnight
The treatment plant stopped producing water
Residents used an entire tank of water in one night of normal use

inference.explanation: Both boosters tripped at 02:00, the tank then drained steadily to empty by 06:00, the lower zone stayed normal, and the dead dialer explains the silence. That is a pump outage draining storage. A break would show water loss or damage rather than a steady level fall, the plant produced normally, and normal use does not empty a zone tank in four hours.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the outage sequence?

options.label: Archived pump station run and fault logs paired with tank level records
Archived main break reports
Archived plant production log

nextClue.explanation: Pump fault logs against tank level show the trip first and the level falling after it.

clueText.nc-a: Logs show the electrical trip at 02:00, both pumps out from that minute, and the tank level falling at the normal demand rate until empty.
clueText.nc-b: No break reports exist for the zone that night.
clueText.nc-c: Production records show the plant filling its own storage normally.

tasks.prompt: Black water complaints arrive from one district the day after a large trunk main was returned to service following repairs.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Samples from affected taps carry fine black particles that a magnet attracts weakly and the lab identifies as manganese and iron oxides.
The returned main had sat drained for a week, then was refilled and put back at full velocity quickly.
Complaints are confined to the district fed by that trunk main; other districts are clear.
Manganese at the plant outlet is at its normal low level.
The water clears progressively as the district mains are flushed in sequence.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Refilling the repaired main at full velocity scoured manganese and iron deposits off its walls into the district water
The reservoir has turned over and is sending manganese to the whole town
The repair crew contaminated the main with soil
The plant manganese removal process has failed

inference.explanation: Black oxide particles match main deposits, the main sat drained then refilled fast, complaints stay in its district, plant manganese is normal, and sequential flushing clears it. That is scoured pipe deposits. Turnover or plant failure would raise plant outlet manganese and affect the whole town, and soil would not be identified as iron and manganese oxides.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the scouring pattern?

options.label: Archived complaint and flushing records from past trunk main returns to service
Archived reservoir temperature profiles
Archived plant manganese results

nextClue.explanation: Past return-to-service records show the same district-limited black water after fast refills.

clueText.nc-a: Past returns show black water in the fed district whenever the main was refilled quickly, and clean returns when it was refilled slowly with controlled flushing.
clueText.nc-b: Reservoir profiles show the lake still stratified, not turned over.
clueText.nc-c: Plant manganese stayed at its low normal level through those events.

tasks.prompt: A single homeowner reports very weak flow at every tap, while both neighbours have full pressure and flow.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A pressure gauge on the homeowner outside tap reads normal static pressure of 380 kPa with all taps closed.
Pressure collapses to under 100 kPa as soon as one tap is opened, and flow is a trickle.
The meter strainer at the property is found packed with grit and scale fragments.
The service line is an older galvanized line known to narrow internally with corrosion scale.
Street main pressure logging for the week is normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The home service line and meter strainer are restricted, so static pressure is normal but flow collapses under demand
The street main pressure is too low for the whole street
The homeowner water meter is registering incorrectly and cutting flow
The treatment plant is not producing enough water

inference.explanation: Static pressure is normal but collapses under flow, the meter strainer is packed, and the old galvanized service is known to narrow, while neighbours and the main are normal. That is a service restriction. A street or plant problem would hit the neighbours, and a registering error alone does not pack a strainer or collapse pressure.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the service restriction pattern?

options.label: Archived single-home low flow investigation results on this street
Archived street main pressure records
Archived plant production records

nextClue.explanation: Past single-home investigations on the street show the same strainer and service findings.

clueText.nc-a: Three past cases on this street with normal static pressure and collapsing flow all traced to scaled galvanized services and packed meter strainers.
clueText.nc-b: Street main pressure has been logged normal all month.
clueText.nc-c: Plant production has exceeded demand every day this month.

tasks.prompt: Customers on one street report milky white water that looks alarming, starting after the local booster station was restarted following maintenance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: In a clear glass, the milkiness rises and clears from the bottom up within a minute, leaving the water sparkling clear.
Tiny bubbles are visible streaming upward in the glass and in a sample jar from the tap.
Chlorine, turbidity, and bacteriological samples from the street all test normal.
Complaints began within an hour of the booster restart, which had involved draining and refilling a section of main.
The milkiness is gone from the street by the next morning without any treatment change.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The milkiness is dissolved air released as fine bubbles after the main was drained and refilled, and it is harmless
The main has been contaminated with a white chemical
The filters at the plant are passing media into the street main
Lime is precipitating throughout the distribution system

inference.explanation: The cloud clears from the bottom up in a minute, bubbles stream upward, all tests are normal, timing follows a drain and refill, and it vanishes overnight. That is entrained air. A chemical or media event would not clear upward in a glass or pass all tests, and lime precipitation would not disappear overnight untreated.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the air explanation?

options.label: Archived complaint investigation notes from past main refills in this area
Archived chemical delivery records
Archived filter inspection reports

nextClue.explanation: Past refill investigations record the same bottom-up clearing test result.

clueText.nc-a: Notes from two past refills record the same milky water clearing from the bottom up in a glass, with normal samples and complaints ending within a day.
clueText.nc-b: No white chemical deliveries or spills are recorded at the plant.
clueText.nc-c: Filter inspections are normal, and media grains would settle, not rise and vanish.

tasks.prompt: A newly built subdivision with only a few homes occupied reports stale, musty-tasting water and low residuals, although the subdivision mains are brand new.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The subdivision mains were sized for 200 homes; only 12 are occupied, so daily demand is a small fraction of design.
Residual at the subdivision far end measures 0.1 mg/L against 0.9 mg/L where its feed leaves the town system.
Flushing the subdivision mains restores residual and taste for about a week, then complaints return.
Water temperature in the subdivision mains runs warm in summer, close to ground temperature.
Bacteriological samples remain satisfactory, and pressures are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Oversized new mains with very low occupancy give very high water age, so residual decays and taste goes stale
The new pipe material is leaching a contaminant into the water
The town is supplying the subdivision with poor quality water
The subdivision mains are leaking treated water away

inference.explanation: Mains built for 200 homes serve 12, residual falls across the subdivision, flushing fixes it for about a week, and the water sits warm. That is extreme water age from low occupancy. Pipe leaching would not be cured temporarily by flushing in this repeating pattern, town water enters at 0.9 mg/L, and no leak evidence is present.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the water age cycle?

options.label: Archived residual monitoring at the subdivision since first occupancy
Archived pipe material certificates
Archived town feed quality results

nextClue.explanation: Monitoring since occupancy shows residual decaying on the flush cycle as homes slowly fill in.

clueText.nc-a: Monitoring shows residual collapsing within a week of every flush in the first year, with the collapse slowing as occupancy climbed past 40 homes.
clueText.nc-b: Pipe certificates show approved materials, and new subdivisions elsewhere did not show the pattern once occupied.
clueText.nc-c: Feed quality at the subdivision entrance has held at 0.9 mg/L.

tasks.prompt: A district metered area shows minimum night flows that have doubled over three months, while daytime demand and billed consumption are unchanged.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Night flow in the district now bottoms out at 4.0 L/s at 03:00, against a historical 1.8 L/s when legitimate night use is minimal.
An acoustic survey crew hears a strong leak noise on one older cast iron street, loudest between two valves.
District pressure is normal, and no surface water or sinkholes have appeared.
No new large customers have connected, and seasonal irrigation does not run at 03:00 in this district.
Step testing that closes sections in sequence drops the night flow sharply when one street section is isolated.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: An undetected underground leak on the older street is losing treated water continuously
Customers have doubled their legitimate night-time water use
The district meter has drifted and is over-reading
A neighbouring district is feeding water backward into this one

inference.explanation: Night flow doubled while billed use is flat, acoustics localize a leak noise, and isolating one street section drops the flow sharply. That is a real leak in that section. Legitimate use would appear in billing, a drifting meter would not respond to section isolation, and backflow between districts would not localize to one street by acoustics.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the leak location pattern?

options.label: Archived step test and acoustic survey results for the district
Archived district meter calibration record
Archived customer billing summaries

nextClue.explanation: Step test and acoustic records together pinpoint the section losing the water.

clueText.nc-a: The archived step test shows the excess night flow disappearing when the one street section is isolated, and acoustics peak midway along it.
clueText.nc-b: The district meter calibrated within 1 percent last quarter.
clueText.nc-c: Billing summaries are flat, confirming the extra water is unmetered loss.

tasks.prompt: During a January cold snap at minus 28 C, several homes on one older street lose water entirely while the main street pressure stays normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Affected homes are served by shallow-buried older service lines on the wind-exposed side of the street.
Homes across the street, with deeper services, still have water.
A trickle of water returns to one affected home after its basement warms and a tap is left dripping.
The street main is buried deep, its pressure and flow test normal, and a hydrant on the street flows fully.
The same street had service freeze-ups during a similar cold snap five years ago.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The shallow household service lines have frozen, while the deep street main is unaffected
The street main has frozen solid
The treatment plant cannot produce enough water in the cold
All the affected homes have burst internal plumbing at the same time

inference.explanation: Only shallow services on the exposed side are out, deeper services across the street work, the deep main and hydrant flow normally, and one service recovers as it warms. That is frozen services. A frozen main would cut the hydrant and the whole street, plant output would affect the town, and simultaneous internal bursts would show flooding rather than a warming recovery.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the freeze pattern?

options.label: Archived service freeze-up records and service depth drawings for the street
Archived main break reports
Archived plant production log

nextClue.explanation: Freeze records and depth drawings show the same shallow services freezing in past cold snaps.

clueText.nc-a: Records from the cold snap five years ago list the same addresses, all with services shallower than the frost depth shown on the drawings.
clueText.nc-b: No main breaks were reported on the street in either event.
clueText.nc-c: Plant production met demand throughout both cold snaps.

tasks.prompt: Every morning the alum metering pump is found running dry and must be re-primed, although it runs perfectly all day once primed.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The pump suction foot valve at the tank was found with debris on its seat and a weak spring.
The suction line drains back toward the tank overnight; its liquid level falls to tank level by morning.
Once primed, a drawdown test shows the pump delivering exactly its set rate.
The discharge check valve tests and holds normally.
Tank level, chemical strength, and raw-water demand are all normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The leaking suction foot valve lets the pump lose its prime overnight
The pump motor is failing and cannot start under load
The discharge line is plugged and pushing chemical back
The alum tank is emptying every night

inference.explanation: The foot valve seat is fouled with a weak spring, the suction line drains back overnight, and the pump delivers perfectly once primed. That is prime loss through the foot valve. A failing motor would not run all day, a plugged discharge would show during the day, and the tank level is normal.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the foot valve pattern?

options.label: Archived priming complaint log and suction valve maintenance history
Archived pump motor electrical test results
Archived discharge pressure trend

nextClue.explanation: The priming log and valve history show morning prime loss tracking this valve condition.

clueText.nc-a: The log shows morning re-priming needed daily for a month, and the same symptom five years ago was cured by replacing this foot valve.
clueText.nc-b: Motor tests are normal, matching its full-day running.
clueText.nc-c: Discharge pressure is normal whenever the pump is primed.

tasks.prompt: A production well delivers less water each year: operators must run the pump longer, and the pumping water level sits deeper than it used to.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Static water level in the well, measured after a full rest weekend, is unchanged from ten years ago.
Pumping water level at the same flow has dropped 6 m over five years, so specific capacity has fallen steadily.
The well discharge carries slimy, rust-coloured deposits, and a downhole camera shows the screen slots coated and partly bridged with growth and scale.
Neighbouring wells in the same aquifer show no change in their specific capacity.
Pump mechanical inspection found the pump itself within wear limits.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The well screen is encrusting and fouling, choking inflow to the well while the aquifer itself is unchanged
The aquifer is being depleted by regional pumping
The pump impellers have worn out
The well casing has collapsed at the bottom

inference.explanation: Static level is unchanged, pumping level at the same flow fell 6 m, the camera shows coated screen slots, and neighbouring wells are unaffected. Inflow through this well screen is choking. Aquifer depletion would lower static levels and hit neighbours, the pump inspected within limits, and a collapse would not present as gradual coating on camera.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms screen fouling progression?

options.label: Archived specific capacity tests and downhole camera surveys for this well
Archived regional water level monitoring
Archived pump overhaul records

nextClue.explanation: Specific capacity tests and camera surveys track the screen condition worsening year by year.

clueText.nc-a: Tests show specific capacity falling steadily for five years while camera surveys show screen coating thickening over the same period.
clueText.nc-b: Regional monitoring shows stable aquifer levels, clearing depletion.
clueText.nc-c: Overhaul records show the pump renewed and still the capacity kept falling.

tasks.prompt: During a real power outage, the plant standby generator cranks slowly and never starts, leaving the plant on battery alarms until utility power returns.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Battery voltage at the generator reads 21 V on a 24 V starting system, and the terminals are heavily corroded.
The battery charger shows a fault light and no output on its meter.
The generator starts immediately when a booster battery pack is connected for a test.
Fuel level, fuel quality, and engine oil all check normal.
Weekly exercise records show the generator runs were logged as passed, but the charger fault light appears in a photo from a month earlier.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The starting batteries have run down because the battery charger has failed, so the generator cannot crank fast enough to start
The generator fuel has gone bad in the tank
The engine itself has seized
The transfer switch prevented the generator from starting

inference.explanation: Battery voltage is low with corroded terminals, the charger shows a fault with no output, and the engine starts at once on a booster pack. The starting power system failed, not the engine. Fuel checks normal, a seized engine would not start on boost, and a transfer switch acts after the generator starts, not before cranking.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the charger failure timeline?

options.label: Archived generator exercise logs and battery charger inspection notes
Archived fuel delivery and testing records
Archived transfer switch test results

nextClue.explanation: Exercise logs and charger notes show how long the charger fault went unnoticed.

clueText.nc-a: Notes show the charger fault light present at three monthly inspections, marked as monitor, while battery voltage slid a little lower each month.
clueText.nc-b: Fuel tested within specification at the last delivery.
clueText.nc-c: Transfer switch tests passed, and the switch can only act once the generator runs.

tasks.prompt: In an outage, the standby generator starts and runs smoothly, but the plant loads never pick up: the building stays dark with the generator running outside.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Generator output voltage and frequency at its breaker are normal and steady.
The automatic transfer switch is found still in the utility position, with its control fuse blown.
Utility power is confirmed off at the service entrance, so the switch had a real reason to transfer.
Manually transferring the switch in a test restores plant power from the generator immediately.
Generator fuel, oil, and cooling all check normal, and the engine carries the test load without strain.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The transfer switch failed to operate because of its blown control fuse, so generator power never reached the plant
The generator is too small to carry the plant load
The generator is producing no output power
The utility power never actually went out

inference.explanation: Generator output is normal, the switch sits in the utility position with a blown control fuse, utility power is truly off, and a manual transfer powers the plant at once. That is a transfer switch control failure. Output exists, capacity carries the load in the test, and the outage was real.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the switch control fault?

options.label: Archived transfer switch test and inspection records
Archived generator load bank test results
Archived utility outage reports

nextClue.explanation: Switch test records show whether the control circuit fault was developing.

clueText.nc-a: The last two annual switch tests note intermittent transfer on the first attempt, attributed to the aging control circuit that has now failed outright.
clueText.nc-b: Load bank results show the generator carrying full rated load comfortably.
clueText.nc-c: Utility reports confirm the outage and its duration.

tasks.prompt: A variable speed pump drive keeps tripping on overtemperature on warm afternoons, shutting down its pump, then runs fine again in the cool of the night.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The drive heatsink temperature climbs steadily through the day and trips at its limit.
The drive cabinet cooling fan is found stopped, its blades fouled with dust, and the cabinet filter is plugged solid.
Electrical room temperature reaches 34 C on the afternoons when trips occur.
Motor current and pump load are within normal limits at the time of the trips.
A portable fan aimed into the open cabinet lets the drive run through a hot afternoon without tripping.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The drive is overheating because its cabinet cooling has failed in a hot room, not because of the pump load
The pump motor is overloading the drive electrically
The drive power electronics have failed permanently
The pump is cavitating and shaking the drive

inference.explanation: Heatsink temperature climbs to the trip limit, the cabinet fan is stopped with a plugged filter, the room hits 34 C, load is normal, and a portable fan cures it. That is failed cabinet cooling. Motor overload is contradicted by normal current, a permanent electronic failure would not be cured by a fan, and cavitation is a hydraulic symptom not seen here.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the cooling pattern?

options.label: Archived drive temperature trends and cabinet filter maintenance records
Archived motor current trend
Archived drive fault code history from the manufacturer service visit

nextClue.explanation: Temperature trends against filter maintenance show trips tracking the cooling neglect.

clueText.nc-a: Trends show heatsink temperatures creeping higher each summer since the filter was last changed three years ago, with trips beginning this season.
clueText.nc-b: Motor current has been flat and normal for years.
clueText.nc-c: The service visit found the power stage healthy and flagged cabinet airflow.

tasks.prompt: A raw-water pump controlled by a pressure transmitter has begun cycling on and off rapidly, wearing its starter, although demand is steady.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A test gauge teed beside the transmitter reads a steady 420 kPa while the transmitter signal swings between 300 and 550 kPa.
The transmitter impulse line is found partly plugged with sediment and trapped air.
When the impulse line is flushed and vented, the transmitter agrees with the test gauge and the cycling stops.
Pump, motor, and check valve all test mechanically sound.
System demand and tank levels were steady through the cycling period.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The pressure transmitter is feeding a false, swinging signal because its impulse line is fouled, and the control is chasing the false signal
The pump has lost capacity and cannot hold pressure
A large leak is opening and closing in the system
The pump check valve is slamming and causing real pressure swings

inference.explanation: A test gauge reads steady while the transmitter swings, its impulse line is plugged with sediment and air, and flushing it restores agreement and stops the cycling. That is a false instrument signal. A weak pump or real swings would show on the test gauge, and a leak would not be cured by cleaning an impulse line.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms impulse line fouling?

options.label: Archived transmitter calibration and impulse line maintenance history
Archived pump performance test results
Archived system leak survey

nextClue.explanation: Transmitter history shows past false signals from the same neglected impulse lines.

clueText.nc-a: History shows two prior erratic-signal events on this transmitter, both cured by flushing impulse lines that had missed their maintenance interval.
clueText.nc-b: Pump tests show the pump meeting its curve, so capacity is not the issue.
clueText.nc-c: The leak survey found no significant system leakage.

tasks.prompt: A high-lift pump has begun rattling like gravel is passing through it, vibrating heavily, and its discharge pressure swings up and down.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The noise and vibration are worst when the wet well level is low and ease when the level rises.
Suction pressure at the pump dips sharply and fluctuates with the noise.
The pump discharge flow swings in step with the pressure swings.
Inspection of a removed suction strainer shows it clear, and the impeller shows pitting damage on its vane surfaces.
Motor current swings with the discharge swings, but electrical tests are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The pump is cavitating: at low suction level it is starved of water, and vapour bubbles collapsing in the impeller are causing the noise, vibration, and pitting
Gravel from the wet well is passing through the pump
The motor bearings have failed and are rattling
The discharge check valve is broken and flapping

inference.explanation: Symptoms track low wet well level, suction pressure dips and fluctuates, the strainer is clear, and the impeller vanes are pitted. That is cavitation damage. Gravel is excluded by the clear strainer, bearing failure would not follow suction level, and a flapping check valve would not pit the impeller vanes.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms cavitation conditions?

options.label: Archived suction level and pump performance records for low-level periods
Archived wet well cleaning records
Archived motor vibration analysis reports

nextClue.explanation: Suction records show performance breaking down whenever level falls below a threshold.

clueText.nc-a: Records show discharge pressure and flow becoming unstable every time wet well level dropped below the pump minimum submergence mark, across three summers.
clueText.nc-b: Wet well cleaning found little debris, and the strainer is clear today.
clueText.nc-c: Vibration analysis shows broadband energy typical of cavitation rather than a bearing tone.

tasks.prompt: After a pump stops, a violent bang shakes its discharge piping, and the pump is sometimes found slowly rotating backward when the crew arrives.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The discharge check valve on this pump is found with its disc separated from its hinge pin, lying in the valve body.
Pressure logging shows a sharp spike in the discharge line at the moment of each pump stop.
Reverse rotation is confirmed by the pump shaft turning backward with the pump off and its twin running.
The twin pump beside it, with an intact check valve, stops quietly with no bang.
Pump motor and starter tests are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The failed check valve lets the discharge column rush back through the pump at shutdown, causing water hammer and reverse rotation
The pump motor starter is reversing the pump electrically
Air trapped in the discharge line is exploding at shutdown
The pump is oversized and always hammers at shutdown

inference.explanation: The check valve disc is detached inside the body, pressure spikes log at each stop, the shaft turns backward, and the twin with an intact valve stops quietly. That is backflow through the failed check. A starter cannot reverse a stopped pump, trapped air would affect the twin line too, and oversizing would not detach a disc or single out this pump.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the check valve failure effect?

options.label: Archived pressure transient logs and check valve inspection history
Archived motor starter maintenance records
Archived pump sizing calculations

nextClue.explanation: Transient logs and valve history tie the hammer spikes to this valve deteriorating.

clueText.nc-a: Logs show shutdown spikes growing over six months on this pump only, and the valve had missed two inspection cycles in that period.
clueText.nc-b: Starter records are normal, and a starter cannot turn a stopped pump backward.
clueText.nc-c: Sizing calculations match the pump to the system, and the twin behaves normally.

tasks.prompt: Several pneumatic valves across a plant have drifted to odd positions and actuators are sluggish on the same morning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Instrument air header pressure reads 380 kPa against a normal 700 kPa.
The air compressor is running continuously but its dryer tower is found saturated, and water drains from the header low points.
Air filters at the actuators are wet and partly plugged.
The compressor intake filter is heavily fouled, and its unload cycle has not operated.
Electrical power to the valves positioners is normal, and the control signals are correct.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The instrument air supply is failing in pressure and quality, so pneumatic actuators across the plant cannot respond properly
Every valve positioner has failed electronically at once
The control system software has corrupted all valve signals
The process water pressure has dropped plant-wide

inference.explanation: Header pressure is barely half of normal, the compressor runs continuously with a saturated dryer, water drains from the header, and actuator filters are wet and plugged, while signals test correct. That is a common air supply failure. Simultaneous electronic failures and software corruption are implausible against correct signals, and process water pressure is a separate system not reported low.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms air system neglect?

options.label: Archived compressor and dryer maintenance records and header pressure trend
Archived positioner diagnostic reports
Archived control system change log

nextClue.explanation: Air system records show dryer and filter maintenance lapsing as header pressure slid.

clueText.nc-a: Records show dryer desiccant and intake filters two years past their change interval, with header pressure trending down over the same period.
clueText.nc-b: Positioner diagnostics run after air was restored show the devices healthy.
clueText.nc-c: The control change log shows no software changes this month.

tasks.prompt: A magnetic flow meter on the plant discharge reads flows about 20 percent higher than the clearwell level changes can account for.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A volume balance over a quiet night shows the meter totalizing about 20 percent more water than the clearwell actually delivered.
The meter electrodes are found coated with a hard mineral film when the spool is inspected.
A portable clamp-on meter on the same pipe reads close to the volume balance value, not the mag meter value.
The meter grounding rings are corroded and one grounding strap is broken.
Pipe flow conditions and pump rates have not changed.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The mag meter is over-reading because its electrodes are coated and its grounding is compromised
The clearwell is leaking 20 percent of its water
The clamp-on meter is the inaccurate instrument
The pumps have suddenly increased their output

inference.explanation: A physical volume balance and an independent clamp-on meter agree against the mag meter, its electrodes are filmed, and a grounding strap is broken. That is meter error from coating and grounding. A clearwell leak of that size would show elsewhere, the clamp-on agrees with the physical balance, and pump rates are unchanged.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the meter drift pattern?

options.label: Archived meter verification and volume balance checks
Archived clearwell structural inspection report
Archived pump curve tests

nextClue.explanation: Verification history shows this meter drifting as its electrodes coated before.

clueText.nc-a: Checks show this meter reading progressively high over a year, resetting to accurate after a past electrode cleaning, and drifting again since.
clueText.nc-b: The clearwell inspection found the structure sound and watertight.
clueText.nc-c: Pump tests show output on curve and unchanged.

tasks.prompt: A chemical storage tank ultrasonic level sensor reports the tank nearly empty and triggers a low-level alarm, yet deliveries have been light and operators believe chemical remains.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A manual dip measurement shows the tank actually about 60 percent full.
The surface of the stored chemical is covered with a layer of foam from a recent delivery agitation.
The sensor reading recovers to match the dip measurement after the foam settles overnight.
The same false low reading occurred right after the previous two deliveries.
Tank vents and the sensor mounting are clear and undamaged.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Foam on the chemical surface is scattering the ultrasonic signal and causing false low level readings after deliveries
The tank really is emptying faster than records show
The sensor has failed permanently and must be replaced
Chemical is leaking from the tank bottom

inference.explanation: The dip shows 60 percent full, foam covers the surface after delivery, the reading recovers as foam settles, and the same false reading followed past deliveries. That is foam interference. A permanent sensor failure would not recover on its own, and a leak or fast use would show in the dip measurement.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the foam pattern?

options.label: Archived level sensor trends around past delivery times
Archived tank integrity test results
Archived chemical usage reconciliation

nextClue.explanation: Sensor trends around deliveries show the false dip and recovery repeating.

clueText.nc-a: Trends show the sensor plunging after each delivery and recovering over the following 12 hours, while manual dips stayed steady.
clueText.nc-b: Integrity tests show the tank sound with no leakage.
clueText.nc-c: Usage reconciliation matches deliveries to consumption within a few percent.

tasks.prompt: A washwater pump for filter backwashing delivers well below its rated flow, so washes have become weak across the plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Discharge pressure and flow are both about 30 percent below the pump curve at the same speed.
Motor current draw is lower than normal, not higher.
Suction supply level and suction piping are normal and clear, and the pump is fully primed.
Inspection through the pump casing port shows impeller vanes heavily worn and rounded, with wide wear ring clearances.
Valves on the discharge line are confirmed fully open.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The pump impeller and wear rings are worn out, so the pump slips internally and can no longer make its rated pressure or flow
The discharge line is throttled by a partly closed valve
The motor is running slow because of an electrical fault
The suction supply is starving the pump

inference.explanation: Pressure and flow are both 30 percent low at full speed, current is low rather than high, the impeller vanes are visibly worn with wide wear ring gaps, and valves and suction are confirmed good. That is internal pump wear. Throttling would raise pressure while cutting flow, a slow motor would show electrically, and the suction checks clear starvation.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms progressive pump wear?

options.label: Archived pump performance test results over the years
Archived valve position inspection log
Archived motor electrical test results

nextClue.explanation: Performance tests over time show the pump curve sagging year by year.

clueText.nc-a: Tests show the pump meeting its curve five years ago and falling a few percent further below it at every test since, the classic wear pattern.
clueText.nc-b: Valve logs confirm discharge valves fully open at each test.
clueText.nc-c: Motor tests show full speed and normal electrical condition.

tasks.prompt: A chlorine metering pump area is found with chemical pooled beneath the pump head, and the plant chlorine dose has fallen off at the same time.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The pump continues to stroke, but its discharge output measured by drawdown is far below setting.
Chemical is weeping from the pump head seam in time with each stroke.
The pump diaphragm leak detector port shows chemical present, which the manual identifies as a ruptured diaphragm sign.
Suction supply, tank level, and injection line all check normal.
A spare pump installed on the same lines restores the dose immediately.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The metering pump diaphragm has ruptured, leaking chemical at the head and losing the dose
The injection line is plugged and forcing chemical out of the tank vent
The chlorine tank has run empty
The pump motor coupling has sheared so the pump is not stroking

inference.explanation: Output is low while stroking, chemical weeps from the head seam with each stroke, the leak detector port shows chemical, and a spare pump on the same lines restores dose. That is a ruptured diaphragm. A plugged line would raise pressure rather than weep at the seam, the tank has chemical, and the pump visibly strokes.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms diaphragm life history?

options.label: Archived diaphragm replacement and pump service records
Archived injection line cleaning log
Archived chlorine tank level records

nextClue.explanation: Service records show the diaphragm age against its expected service life.

clueText.nc-a: Records show this diaphragm at twice its recommended replacement interval, with a note that the last scheduled change was deferred.
clueText.nc-b: Injection line cleaning is current, and the spare pump works through it.
clueText.nc-c: Tank levels show ample chemical throughout the event.

tasks.prompt: A raw-water pump motor has developed a growing rumble over two months, and the crew wants the cause identified before it fails outright.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Vibration readings at the motor bearing housing have tripled over two months and are still climbing.
The bearing housing runs hot to the touch compared with the identical twin motor beside it.
Grease purged from the bearing is dark and contains fine metallic particles.
Pump hydraulic performance, alignment check, and coupling condition all test normal.
The rumble pitch rises and falls exactly with motor speed.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The motor bearing is wearing out, shown by rising vibration, heat, and metal particles in its grease
The pump is cavitating and the noise is hydraulic
The pump and motor have fallen out of alignment
The motor cooling fan has come loose

inference.explanation: Vibration tripled at the bearing housing, the housing runs hot against its twin, grease carries metal particles, and hydraulics and alignment test normal. That is bearing wear. Cavitation would not put metal in motor grease, misalignment was checked normal, and a loose fan would not produce bearing heat and metallic grease.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms bearing deterioration?

options.label: Archived vibration trend and grease analysis history for this motor
Archived alignment records
Archived pump performance tests

nextClue.explanation: Vibration and grease history track the bearing condition worsening over time.

clueText.nc-a: Trends show bearing fault frequencies emerging and growing over two months, and grease analysis iron content doubling between samples.
clueText.nc-b: Alignment was verified in tolerance last month.
clueText.nc-c: Pump performance is on curve, clearing a hydraulic source.

tasks.prompt: Raw-water flow into a northern plant falls off sharply during a bitter cold, still night, although the river level is normal and the intake pumps are healthy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The differential level across the intake screen has risen sharply, showing the screen is obstructing flow.
Divers and a camera find the screen coated with a thick layer of slushy, needle-like ice crystals.
River water temperature measures 0.1 C, just at the point where frazil ice forms in supercooled water.
The same flow loss happened on the last two bitter, still nights and recovered as the days warmed slightly.
Intake pump tests show the pumps meeting their curves on a clear test line.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Frazil ice is coating and plugging the intake screen in the supercooled river water
The intake pipe has frozen solid through its whole length
The river has dropped below the intake level
The intake pumps have lost capacity from wear

inference.explanation: Screen differential is up, the camera shows slushy needle ice coating the screen, the water is at frazil-forming temperature, and the pattern follows bitter still nights and recovers with warming. That is frazil ice on the screen. A fully frozen pipe would not recover daily, river level is normal, and pumps test on curve.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the frazil ice pattern?

options.label: Archived intake differential and river temperature records from past winters
Archived intake pipe inspection report
Archived pump performance tests

nextClue.explanation: Past winter records tie flow loss to supercooled water and screen differential.

clueText.nc-a: Records show intake differential spiking on every night the river hit 0.1 C with calm conditions, and clearing as temperatures eased, in three past winters.
clueText.nc-b: Pipe inspection found the intake pipe clear and full diameter.
clueText.nc-c: Pump tests after each event showed the pumps on curve.
